subject: polsci
book: Contemporary World Politics; Politics in India since Independence (NCERT, rationalised)

chapters.title: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity

sections.name: 1.1 The Berlin Wall and the end of the Cold War

concepts.text: Berlin Wall (built 1961) as the symbol of Cold War division; its fall in November 1989
German unification (1990) and the end of bipolarity
Meaning of a bipolar world vs a unipolar world
USSR born of the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution, inspired by socialist ideals
Second World: East European states in the Soviet bloc, bound by the Warsaw Pact
Features: state ownership, centralised planning, rule of the Communist Party alone
Achievements: industrial and military strength, basic living standard, no unemployment
Weaknesses: bureaucratic and authoritarian rule, lack of freedom, technological lag
Russian dominance over other republics; arms race and the 1979 Afghanistan intervention drained resources
Mikhail Gorbachev became leader in 1985
Reforms: perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness)
East European countries overthrew communist governments in 1989
Failed hardliner coup of 1991 and the rise of Boris Yeltsin
December 1991: Russia, Ukraine and Belarus end the USSR; Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) formed
Russia as successor state, inheriting the UN Security Council seat

sections.name: 1.4 Why did the Soviet Union disintegrate?

concepts.text: Internal weakness of political and economic institutions
Economic stagnation, consumer shortages, cost of the arms race and of satellite states
Gorbachev's reforms raised expectations they could not satisfy; opposed by both reformers and hardliners
Rise of nationalism and sovereignty demands in the republics (Baltic states, Ukraine, Georgia)
End of Cold War confrontation and the arms race
Shift in the power balance: US as sole superpower (unipolarity)
Dominance of capitalism and liberal democracy; greater influence of IMF and World Bank
Emergence of new states: Baltic, East European and Central Asian republics
Shock therapy: sudden switch from authoritarian socialism to democratic capitalism
Elements: privatisation, free trade, currency convertibility, breaking up collective farms
Model pushed by the World Bank and IMF; reorientation of trade toward the West
Economic collapse: state industries sold off at low prices ('largest garage sale in history')
Fall in the value of the rouble, high inflation, collapse of collective farms and food security
Rising inequality, emergence of a mafia, collapse of the old welfare system
Hastily built democracies: strong presidents, weak parliaments
Secessionist wars in Russia: Chechnya and Dagestan
Break-up of Yugoslavia; conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Kosovo; NATO intervention
Conflicts in the former republics: Tajikistan civil war, Armenia-Azerbaijan (Nagorno-Karabakh), Georgia
Central Asian oil and gas reserves attract great-power competition
Close India-USSR ties during the Cold War (1971 Treaty of Peace and Friendship)
India-Russia relations rest on a shared vision of a multipolar world
Areas of cooperation: defence, energy (oil, nuclear), space, trade
India's links with Central Asian states for energy and connectivity
Exercise type: list features of the Soviet system; order events by date; consequences of shock therapy

chapters.title: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power

concepts.text: After the Cold War, regional groupings and rising states act as alternative centres to US dominance
Economic strength and regional integration as sources of influence
Post-war European integration: Marshall Plan, OEEC (1948), Council of Europe (1949)
European Economic Community (1957) to European Union through the Maastricht Treaty (1992)
Single market, common currency (euro, 2002), common foreign and security policy
EU as an economic, political and military power; France holds a permanent UN Security Council seat
Limits: members keep separate foreign policies; Euroscepticism; Brexit (UK left in 2020)
EU symbols: flag with a circle of gold stars
ASEAN founded in 1967 (Bangkok Declaration) by Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore and Thailand
'ASEAN Way': informal, non-confrontational, cooperative style
ASEAN Community (2003): security, economic and socio-cultural pillars
ASEAN Regional Forum (1994) for security dialogue
ASEAN Free Trade Area and economic growth; India's Look East / Act East policy
ASEAN Vision 2020 and its outward-looking role in the region
After 1949 China followed a Soviet-style state-controlled economy
Reforms under Deng Xiaoping from 1978: open door policy
Privatisation of agriculture (1982) and industry (1998); Special Economic Zones
China's WTO entry (2001) and rise as a global economic power
Problems: unemployment, environmental damage, corruption, inequality
China's growing regional influence and ties with neighbours
Old cultural links; the 1962 conflict damaged relations
Normalisation after Rajiv Gandhi's 1988 visit; fast-growing trade
Border disputes and rivalry alongside cooperation in multilateral forums

sections.name: 2.6 Japan and South Korea as emerging powers

concepts.text: Japan: technological and economic power despite few natural resources; G-7 member
Japan's military limited by Article 9 of its Constitution; a major funder of the UN
South Korea: rapid growth ('Miracle on the Han River'); member of OECD and G-20
Exercise type: compare EU and ASEAN; features of China's economic reforms
South Asia: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka (Afghanistan often included)
Geographic unity (Himalayas, Indian Ocean) amid diverse political systems
Map work: locate South Asian countries and capitals

sections.name: 3.2 The Military and Democracy in Pakistan

concepts.text: Military rule: Ayub Khan, Yahya Khan, Zia-ul-Haq, Pervez Musharraf
Reasons for weak democracy: army, clergy and landlord dominance; Cold War US backing
Periods of elected government with continued army influence
East Pakistan until 1971; Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and the Awami League
Liberation War of 1971 with Indian support
Shifts between presidential rule and multi-party parliamentary democracy (since 1991)
Nepal as a Hindu kingdom and later a constitutional monarchy
People's movements of 1990 and 2006; Maoist insurgency
Monarchy abolished in 2008; new Constitution in 2015

sections.name: 3.5 Ethnic Conflict and Democracy in Sri Lanka

concepts.text: Sinhala majoritarianism and the Tamil question
LTTE and the demand for Tamil Eelam; civil war ending in 2009
Indian Peace Keeping Force (1987-90)
Sri Lanka's economic growth and high human development despite conflict
Kashmir as the core dispute; wars of 1947-48, 1965, 1971 and Kargil (1999)
Siachen glacier, Sir Creek and river water sharing (Indus Waters Treaty)
1998 nuclear tests, arms race and cross-border terrorism
India-Bangladesh: Ganga waters, migration and border issues alongside cooperation
India-Nepal: open border, trade and occasional friction
India-Sri Lanka: Tamil issue, trade and cooperation
India-Bhutan friendship; India-Maldives ties (Operation Cactus, 1988)
SAARC set up in 1985 for regional cooperation
SAFTA (South Asian Free Trade Area) agreement, 2004
SAARC's limits because of India-Pakistan tensions
Influence of external powers (USA, China) in South Asia
Exercise type: compare democracy across South Asian states; evaluate SAARC

sections.name: 4.1 Meaning and importance of International Organisations

concepts.text: International organisations help states cooperate on war, peace and shared problems
They supply rules, forums and information for collective action
Failure of the League of Nations; UN founded in 1945 (Charter signed by 51 states)
UN aims: prevent conflict, foster cooperation and social-economic development
Membership now 193 states
Organs: General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, International Court of Justice, Secretariat, Trusteeship Council
Security Council: 5 permanent members with veto, 10 elected non-permanent members
Role of the Secretary-General; list of Secretaries-General
Specialised agencies and bodies: WHO, UNDP, UNHRC, UNHCR, UNICEF, UNESCO

sections.name: 4.4 Reform of the UN after the Cold War

concepts.text: Why reform: more members, unipolarity, new challenges
Reform of structures and processes: expanding the Security Council
Proposed criteria for new permanent members
Reform of jurisdiction: peacekeeping, terrorism, human rights, climate
2005 decisions: Peacebuilding Commission, Human Rights Council, Democracy Fund
India backs restructuring of the UN and an enlarged Security Council
India's case for a permanent seat: population, economy, peacekeeping record, democracy
Objections and debates about India's candidature

sections.name: 4.6 The UN in a Unipolar World

concepts.text: US influence in the UN through funding, veto and power
UN remains a forum for dialogue despite its limits
IMF: oversees the international financial system; votes weighted by contributions
World Bank: development loans and grants; criticism of its conditions
WTO (1995, successor to GATT): sets rules of global trade
IAEA (1957): promotes peaceful nuclear energy and runs inspections
ILO: labour standards and workers' rights
NGOs: Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch
Implications and future of international organisations
Exercise type: match organisations with functions; arguments on Security Council reform

chapters.title: World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World

concepts.text: Security as freedom from threats to a society's core values
Threats serious enough to endanger survival and justify extraordinary steps
Military threat from other states as the main danger
Options: surrender, deterrence (preventing war) or defence (limiting war)
Balance of power and alliance building
Use of force in pursuit of national interest
Internal threats: separatist movements and insurgency
Post-colonial states face internal conflicts more than external wars
Disarmament: giving up classes of weapons (BWC 1972, CWC 1992)
Arms control: regulating weapons (ABM Treaty 1972, SALT, START)
NPT (1968) and why India calls it discriminatory
Confidence-building measures to prevent conflict
Human security: protecting people rather than territory
Narrow vs broad human security: freedom from fear and from want
Global security: threats such as global warming and pandemics that affect everyone
Terrorism: political violence against civilians (e.g. 9/11)
Human rights violations and the humanitarian intervention debate
Global poverty and the North-South gap
Migration, refugees and internally displaced persons
Health epidemics: HIV-AIDS, bird flu, SARS, COVID-19
Non-traditional threats need international cooperation
Role of international bodies, NGOs and businesses
Force as a last resort when cooperation fails
Building military capability, including nuclear tests (1974, 1998)
Strengthening international norms and institutions: NAM, disarmament, UN peacekeeping
Handling internal security challenges (Nagaland, Mizoram, Punjab, Kashmir)
Economic development to lift people out of poverty
Exercise type: contrast traditional and non-traditional security; identify parts of India's strategy

chapters.title: World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources

concepts.text: Global problems: land degradation, water scarcity, deforestation, ozone depletion, coastal pollution
Club of Rome's 'Limits to Growth' (1972); UNEP
Brundtland Report 'Our Common Future' (1987) and sustainable development
UN Conference on Environment and Development, Rio de Janeiro (1992)
Outcomes: Agenda 21, conventions on climate change and biodiversity, Rio Declaration
Global North vs Global South views on environment and development
Global commons: atmosphere, Antarctica, ocean floor, outer space
Antarctic Treaty (1959), Montreal Protocol (1987), Antarctic Environmental Protocol (1991)
Why cooperation over commons is hard
Developed countries bear more responsibility because of historical emissions
UNFCCC (1992); Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the exemption of India and China
Paris Agreement and the continuing North-South debate
Resources owned and managed by a community (e.g. sacred groves)
Decline due to privatisation, population pressure and intensive farming
India signed the Kyoto Protocol in 2002; stresses low per-capita emissions
Domestic steps: Auto-fuel Policy, Energy Conservation Act 2001, Electricity Act 2003, National Action Plan on Climate Change
India's position at summits: developed countries must lead
Forest movements across the Global South, including India
Movements against mining industries (e.g. Philippines, Australia)
Anti-dam movements; Narmada Bachao Andolan
Competition over who gets which resources, when and how
Oil: West Asian reserves and global politics
Water: conflicts over shared rivers and freshwater
Claims of indigenous peoples to land, culture and self-government
World Council of Indigenous Peoples (1975); UN working group on indigenous populations
Exercise type: explain CBDR; India's environmental stand; examples of global commons
Globalisation: worldwide flows of ideas, capital, goods and people
Multi-dimensional: political, economic and cultural sides
Interconnectedness with uneven effects across countries and groups
Technology: telegraph, telephone, microchip, internet
Fast movement of ideas, capital and goods due to technological change
Historical roots in trade and colonialism
Weakening of state capacity: shift from welfare state to minimalist state
State still central for law and order and security
Technology also boosts the state's capacity to gather information
Economic globalisation: more trade and investment, fewer restrictions
Role of IMF, WTO and multinational corporations
Debate on winners and losers; inequality and social safety nets
Cultural homogenisation: spread of Western/American culture ('McDonaldisation')
Cultural heterogenisation: hybrid cultures, e.g. blue jeans worn with a khadi kurta
Colonial-era integration and post-independence protectionism
1991 economic reforms: liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation
Effects on growth, employment and inequality
Critics from the left (inequality) and the right (loss of culture and sovereignty)
World Social Forum as a global platform of opposition
Resistance in India: unions, farmers, campaigns against foreign goods and cultural influences
Exercise type: classify consequences of globalisation; evaluate India's experience

chapters.title: Politics in India: Challenges of Nation Building

concepts.text: Independence on 14-15 August 1947; Nehru's 'Tryst with Destiny' speech
Three challenges: unity and integrity, democracy, development with justice
Two-nation theory and the demand for Pakistan
Process of Partition: Muslim-majority areas, East and West Pakistan, division of Punjab and Bengal
Difficulties: no single Muslim-majority belt, minorities on both sides, princely states
Consequences: communal violence, mass migration, abduction of women, division of assets
Rehabilitation of refugees and the new state's secular commitment
The problem: 565 princely states could join India or Pakistan or stay independent
Government's approach led by Sardar Patel (with V.P. Menon)
Instrument of Accession signed by most rulers
Hyderabad: Nizam's resistance, Razakars, peasant struggle, police action (1948)
Manipur: accession in 1949 despite an elected Assembly
Junagadh and Kashmir as special cases
Linguistic state demands; Potti Sriramulu's fast and death; creation of Andhra Pradesh (1953)
States Reorganisation Commission (1953) and States Reorganisation Act (1956)
Later changes: Gujarat and Maharashtra (1960), Punjab and Haryana (1966), Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura (1972)
Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand (2000) and Telangana (2014)
Linguistic states strengthened unity by accommodating diversity
Exercise type: map work on princely states and new states; true/false on Partition

chapters.title: Politics in India: Era of One-Party Dominance

concepts.text: India chose democracy with universal adult franchise despite poverty and illiteracy
Election Commission set up in 1950; first CEC Sukumar Sen
First general election 1951-52 as a huge exercise; voting methods from ballot boxes to EVMs

sections.name: 9.2 Congress Dominance in the First Three General Elections

concepts.text: Congress won large majorities in 1952, 1957 and 1962
First-past-the-post magnified Congress's seat share over its vote share
Communist government in Kerala (1957) under E.M.S. Namboodiripad as an exception
One-party dominance in India came under democratic conditions (unlike, e.g., Mexico's PRI)
Rooted in the legacy of the national movement and a wide organisation

sections.name: 9.4 Congress as Social and Ideological Coalition

concepts.text: Congress brought together peasants and industrialists, town and village, many castes
Accommodated socialists, conservatives and radicals
Factions inside Congress acted like an internal opposition
Coalition-style party culture tolerated differences
Socialist Party: Acharya Narendra Dev, Ram Manohar Lohia, Jayaprakash Narayan
Communist Party of India: A.K. Gopalan, S.A. Dange
Bharatiya Jana Sangh (1951): Syama Prasad Mookerjee; cultural nationalism
Swatantra Party (1959): C. Rajagopalachari; pro-free market
Role of opposition: criticism and keeping the ruling party accountable
Exercise type: match parties with leaders; explain Congress dominance

chapters.title: Politics in India: Politics of Planned Development

concepts.text: Development decisions involve clashing interests (e.g. mining vs environment and tribal rights)
Example: debate over iron-ore mining and steel plants in Odisha
Development understood as becoming 'modern' like industrial nations
Two models: liberal-capitalist (US) and socialist (USSR)
Left and right positions on the role of the state in the economy
Broad consensus for planning; Bombay Plan (1944) by industrialists
Planning Commission set up in 1950, chaired by the PM
Five Year Plans: government sets income and spending priorities for five years
Planning Commission replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015
First Five Year Plan (1951-56): agriculture, dams and irrigation; K.N. Raj
Second Five Year Plan (1956-61): rapid heavy industrialisation; P.C. Mahalanobis
Public sector and import substitution; mixed economy
Exercise type: compare First and Second Plans; explain the development models

chapters.title: Politics in India: India's External Relations

concepts.text: Newly independent India in a Cold War world
Article 51 (Directive Principles) on promoting international peace and security
Nehru as PM and foreign minister shaped foreign policy
Goals: sovereignty, territorial integrity, rapid economic development
Distance from the two camps: no military alliance with US or USSR
Afro-Asian unity: Asian Relations Conference (1947), Bandung Conference (1955)
NAM founded at Belgrade (1961) with Nehru, Tito and Nasser
Panchsheel agreement (1954): five principles of peaceful coexistence
Tibet issue and asylum for the Dalai Lama (1959)
Chinese aggression of 1962 and India's defeat; impact on Nehru and domestic politics
Later India-China normalisation
Kashmir conflict (1947-48) and UN involvement
Indus Waters Treaty (1960)
1965 war and the Tashkent Agreement (1966)
Bangladesh War (1971): East Pakistan crisis, Indo-Soviet Treaty, Shimla Agreement (1972)
Kargil conflict (1999)
Nehru's opposition to nuclear weapons; Homi J. Bhabha and the atomic energy programme
Nuclear tests at Pokhran in 1974 and 1998
India rejects the NPT and CTBT as discriminatory
Nuclear doctrine: no first use and credible minimum deterrence
Exercise type: order foreign policy events by date; explain NAM and its relevance

chapters.title: Politics in India: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System

concepts.text: Nehru to Shastri (1964): smooth succession; 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan'
Shastri's death at Tashkent (1966) and the choice of Indira Gandhi
Role of the 'Syndicate' of senior Congress leaders and K. Kamaraj
Context: economic crisis, rupee devaluation, drought and food shortages
Non-Congressism: Ram Manohar Lohia's strategy to unite the opposition
Electoral verdict: a 'political earthquake'; Congress lost several states
Coalitions: Samyukta Vidhayak Dal governments in states
Defections and 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram' politics
Indira Gandhi vs the Syndicate: struggle for control of the party
Ten-point programme and bank nationalisation (1969)
Presidential election 1969: V.V. Giri vs N. Sanjeeva Reddy; 'conscience vote'
Split into Congress (O) and Congress (R)
Abolition of privy purses of former princes

sections.name: 12.4 The 1971 Election and Restoration of Congress

concepts.text: Grand Alliance's 'Indira hatao' vs Indira Gandhi's 'Garibi hatao'
Outcome: sweeping Congress (R) victory
Restoration of Congress dominance around a single leader
Popularity boost from the 1971 Bangladesh war victory
Exercise type: order events of 1964-71 by date; explain the Congress split

chapters.title: Politics in India: The Crisis of Democratic Order

concepts.text: Economic context: costs of the 1971 war, oil price rise, inflation, unemployment
Gujarat movement (1974) of students against corruption and price rise
Bihar movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan; call for 'Total Revolution'
Nationwide railway strike (1974) led by George Fernandes
Conflict with the judiciary: Kesavananda Bharati case and supersession of judges (1973)
Allahabad High Court ruling (12 June 1975) setting aside Indira Gandhi's election (Raj Narain case)
Emergency declared on 25 June 1975 under Article 352 citing 'internal disturbance'
Crisis and response: mass arrests of opposition leaders and press censorship
Ban on organisations such as RSS and Jamaat-e-Islami
Preventive detention (MISA) and the ADM Jabalpur habeas corpus case
Effects on civil liberties and the independence of courts
42nd Amendment (1976): longer Lok Sabha term, curbs on courts
Excesses: forced sterilisation, slum demolitions; Shah Commission inquiry
Showed how hard it is to abolish democracy in India
Emergency ground changed from 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' (44th Amendment)
Greater awareness of civil liberties and civil society
1977 Lok Sabha elections: Congress defeated; Janata Party formed government
Janata government under Morarji Desai, then Charan Singh; infighting and collapse
Congress returned to power in 1980
Legacy: anti-Congress politics and rise of backward-class politics
Exercise type: causes and consequences of the Emergency; evaluate its lessons
Indian approach: accommodate regional demands through democratic means
Areas of tension: J&K, Punjab, North-East and linguistic/regional demands
Balancing national unity with regional diversity
Roots of the problem: Maharaja Hari Singh, tribal invasion from Pakistan, accession (1947)
External and internal disputes: Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (POJK); demands for autonomy
Politics since 1948: Sheikh Abdullah and the National Conference
Insurgency and after: 1987 elections and the rise of militancy
2002 and beyond: elections and coalition governments
Abrogation of Article 370 (2019) and creation of the UTs of J&K and Ladakh
Political context: Akali Dal and the Punjabi Suba (1966)
Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973) seeking greater autonomy
Cycle of violence: militancy, Operation Blue Star (1984), Indira Gandhi's assassination, anti-Sikh violence
Road to peace: Rajiv Gandhi-Longowal Accord (1985) and normalcy in the 1990s
The 'seven sisters': geography, isolation and ethnic diversity
Demands for autonomy and creation of new states (Meghalaya, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh)
Secessionist movements: Mizo National Front under Laldenga and the Mizoram Accord (1986); Naga movement under Phizo
Movements against outsiders: Assam Movement (1979-85) led by AASU; Assam Accord (1985)
Assam and national integration
Lessons: democratic negotiation, power-sharing and balanced economic development
Regional aspirations are part of democratic politics, not anti-national
Exercise type: map work on regions; match movements with leaders and accords

chapters.title: Politics in India: Recent Developments in Indian Politics

concepts.text: Rajiv Gandhi's assassination (1991) and decline of Congress
Key developments: Mandal issue, New Economic Policy (1991), Ayodhya movement
End of Congress dominance and rise of multi-party competition
National Front government (1989) under V.P. Singh
United Front governments (1996-98): H.D. Deve Gowda, I.K. Gujral
NDA government under Atal Bihari Vajpayee (1998-2004)
UPA governments under Manmohan Singh (2004-14)
Coalition and alliance politics as the norm from 1989 to 2014

sections.name: 15.3 Political Rise of Other Backward Classes

concepts.text: Mandal Commission (set up 1978): recommended 27% reservation for OBCs
Implementation in 1990 by the V.P. Singh government and the protests that followed
Indra Sawhney case (1992) upheld OBC reservation
Political fallout: rise of the BSP (Kanshi Ram) and other OBC/Dalit-based parties
Ram Janmabhoomi movement and its impact on national politics
Demolition of the three-domed structure at Ayodhya (December 1992)
Supreme Court verdict (2019) and construction of the Ram temple
From legal proceedings to amicable acceptance of the verdict
Lok Sabha elections 2004-2019: BJP majority in 2014 and 2019
Growing consensus: economic policy, OBC claims, role of state parties, pragmatic alliances
Exercise type: order coalition governments by date; explain the political impact of Mandal
